name: Potstill Brandy
description: South African brandy made to rules stricter than cognac's: at least thirty per cent pot-distilled, three years minimum in oak, and no shortcuts permitted. The country has been quietly winning international brandy awards for decades.
funFact: South Africa's first brandy was distilled aboard a ship in Table Bay in 1672 by a cook who described the result, in the log, as unimpressive.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature. South Africans also drink it long with cola as a brandy and Coke, which is a national habit and not one to be sniffy about, though the pot-still bottlings deserve better.

composition.summary: Chenin and Colombard wine pot-distilled and aged in French oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Chenin Blanc and Colombard from the Western Cape

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, minimum 30% of the blend

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak casks under 340 litres

composition.process: The three-year minimum applies to every drop, not just the youngest component, which is stricter than most brandy law.

name: Witblits
description: White lightning, in Afrikaans: unaged grape spirit distilled on Cape farms and traditionally sold in whatever bottle came to hand. Clear, fierce and increasingly made with real care by producers who used to hide it.
funFact: Witblits was farm-distilled for generations under a system of home-production rights, and only became a legally recognised category relatively recently.

serve.how: Cool and neat in small measures, which is how Cape farmers take it. The better modern bottlings are clean enough to drink like a good eau-de-vie; the farm stuff is not, and does not pretend to be.

composition.summary: Grapes or pomace fermented and pot-distilled, unaged.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often on the farm

composition.process: Ageing it in wood makes something else entirely, which is why the category is defined by the absence of colour.

name: Mampoer
description: South African farm fruit brandy, made from peach, apricot, marula or prickly pear depending on the season. The name is said to come from a Pedi chief, and the drink has a reputation for potency that it earns.
funFact: Herman Charles Bosman's short stories made mampoer a fixture of South African literature long before it was legally regulated.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, at room temperature. Peach and apricot are the classics. Like witblits, quality is entirely down to the maker, and the good stuff smells of the fruit rather than of alcohol.

composition.summary: Farm fruit fermented and pot-distilled without additives.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Peach, apricot, marula, prickly pear or plum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, small farm batches

composition.process: Mampoer is distilled from whole fruit while witblits comes from grapes, which is the distinction between the two.

name: Amarula
description: Cream liqueur made from the marula fruit, which is fermented and distilled before the cream goes in. The elephants on the label refer to a widely repeated story about them eating fallen fruit and getting drunk, which is mostly a myth.
funFact: Marula fruit is gathered from wild trees by rural communities rather than farmed, since the trees are protected and notoriously difficult to cultivate.

serve.how: Over ice, or poured over ice cream. It also goes into coffee well. Serve it properly cold; at room temperature the cream flattens and the fruit disappears underneath it.

composition.summary: Marula fruit fermented, distilled, oak-aged, then blended with cream.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Marula fruit spirit, distilled from the fermented fruit

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Fruit fermented and distilled before blending

components.label: Aging
components.detail: The spirit spends two years in oak before the cream is added

composition.process: Unlike most cream liqueurs the base is a genuine fruit distillate rather than neutral spirit.

name: Van der Hum
description: A Cape tangerine liqueur made since the seventeenth century, built on brandy and flavoured with naartjie peel and spice. One of the oldest continuously made liqueurs outside Europe.
funFact: The name translates roughly as what's-his-name, apparently because the Dutch settler who first made it could not be recalled by the person who named it.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice. It is also used in Cape cooking, particularly in desserts and with dried fruit. A splash in a brandy Old Fashioned is a very good idea.

composition.summary: Cape brandy infused with naartjie peel and spices.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Naartjie (tangerine) peel, nutmeg, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves

composition.process: The naartjie is a Cape citrus variety, and using its dried peel rather than the juice is what keeps it dry.

name: Cape Gin
description: South African gin built on fynbos, the shrubland flora of the Cape that exists nowhere else on earth. Buchu, rooibos, honeybush and kapokbos give it a dusty, herbal quality no European gin can imitate.
funFact: The Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of the world's six floral kingdoms and the only one contained entirely within a single country.

serve.glass: Large copa with plenty of ice
serve.how: With a neutral tonic and a rosemary sprig or grapefruit peel, so the fynbos comes through rather than being buried. Skip the cucumber and lime; they flatten exactly the botanicals you are paying for.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with juniper and Cape fynbos botanicals.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper plus buchu, rooibos, honeybush, kapokbos, wild rosemary

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with vapour baskets for delicate botanicals

composition.process: Grape-based neutral spirit is common here, since the Cape has more wine than grain.

name: Mahia
description: Fig or date distillate kept alive for centuries by Moroccan Jewish families, and now made by very few people anywhere. Clear, dry and faintly aniseed, and among the most endangered spirits in this list.
funFact: Most of Morocco's Jewish community emigrated in the mid-twentieth century, and the surviving mahia tradition now runs largely through Israel and France.

serve.how: Cool and neat, in a small glass, with salted food. It is traditionally drunk at celebrations and on Shabbat, and the aniseed versions are the ones most people encounter.

composition.summary: Figs or dates fermented and distilled, sometimes with anise.
composition.process: Figs ferment readily but yield little alcohol, so a great weight of fruit goes into every bottle.

name: Boukha
description: Tunisian fig brandy, clear and unaged, developed in the late nineteenth century by the country's Jewish community. Drier and cleaner than most fruit brandies, and drunk cold rather than contemplated.
funFact: The name comes from an Arabic word for vapour, referring to the steam rising off the still.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small glass, before or after a meal. Tunisians also pour it over melon or fresh figs, which is an excellent use of both.

composition.summary: Mediterranean figs fermented and double-distilled.
composition.process: Only figs and water go in; there is no added sugar or flavouring in a genuine boukha.

name: Thibarine
description: A date and herb liqueur made at Thibar in northern Tunisia, originally by White Fathers missionaries who planted vines and orchards in the hills. Sweet, spiced and increasingly hard to find.
funFact: The monastery at Thibar ran a substantial agricultural estate under the French protectorate, and the liqueur outlived the mission that created it.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice with a strip of orange peel. It is sweet and heavily spiced, so a small pour does the work. Also good stirred into mint tea, oddly enough.

composition.summary: Date distillate blended with herbs, spices and sugar.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Herbs and spices to a monastic recipe

composition.process: The recipe was developed by missionaries who applied European liqueur technique to North African fruit.

name: Zibib
description: Egypt's anise spirit, related to arak and ouzo and clouding the same way with water. The name comes from the Arabic for raisin, which is what much of it is distilled from.
funFact: Egyptian bars serve it with a small jug of water so drinkers can watch the louche happen at the table, which is half the ritual.

serve.how: Poured over ice or cut with two parts water, which turns it milky white. Egyptians drink it with mezze rather than after a meal, and it stands up well to strongly spiced food.

composition.summary: Grape or raisin spirit redistilled with aniseed.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the anise, usually twice

composition.process: Anethole precipitating out of solution when water is added is what produces the cloud.

name: Areke
description: Ethiopian grain spirit distilled from barley, maize or teff and flavoured with gesho, the buckthorn leaf that also bitters the country's beer. Made at home across the highlands and served at every celebration.
funFact: Gesho, Rhamnus prinoides, is Ethiopia's hop equivalent and has been used in brewing and distilling there for centuries.

serve.how: Neat and at room temperature, poured for guests at weddings, holidays and mourning gatherings alike. It is a household product, and the strength varies dramatically depending on who made it.

composition.summary: Grain fermented with gesho and distilled in clay or metal stills.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Gesho leaf, which also drives fermentation

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Simple pot stills, often clay, sometimes twice

composition.process: Double-distilled areke is called dagim and is noticeably cleaner than the single-run version.

name: Aragi
description: Sudanese date spirit, distilled quietly and at some risk in a country where alcohol has been prohibited since 1983. Made from the date palms that line the Nile, and the tradition long predates the ban.
funFact: Sudan removed the death penalty for alcohol consumption by non-Muslims in 2020, a change that made the trade marginally less dangerous.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and discreetly. It is a homemade spirit sold through informal networks, and quality varies with the maker's skill and equipment.

composition.summary: Dates fermented and distilled in improvised stills.
composition.process: Dates are high in sugar and ferment readily, which is why they became the region's distilling crop.

name: Chang'aa
description: Kenyan maize and millet moonshine, illegal until 2010 and still made mostly outside any regulation. The name means kill me quick, and adulterated batches have killed people, which is precisely why it was legalised.
funFact: Kenya legalised and set standards for chang'aa in 2010 specifically to pull production out of the informal sector, where methanol adulteration had caused mass poisonings.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and only from a licensed producer. The legalised bottled versions are safe; the informal ones are a genuine gamble, and that distinction matters more here than anywhere else in this list.

composition.summary: Maize, millet or sorghum fermented and pot-distilled.
composition.process: The legal standard sets a methanol limit, which is the entire point of the regulation.

name: Kenya Cane
description: Kenya's licensed cane spirit, clean and light, and the country's answer to white rum. It sits on every bar shelf from Nairobi to Mombasa and is drunk mostly with soda and lime.
funFact: It has been produced since the 1960s and is one of the few East African spirits with genuine brand recognition across the region.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and lime, or with coconut water. It is a light mixing spirit rather than a sipping one, and it substitutes cleanly for white rum in almost anything.

composition.summary: Kenyan cane molasses fermented and column-distilled.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None for the white; a coconut-flavoured version exists

composition.process: Kenya's sugar belt around Kisumu supplies the molasses that goes into it.

name: Waragi
description: Ugandan spirit distilled from bananas, millet or cassava, made across the country in village stills. The name is a corruption of war gin, from the spirit issued to soldiers during the Second World War.
funFact: Banana waragi, made from the local matoke varieties, is distinct enough from the millet version that Ugandans treat them as separate drinks.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures. Village waragi is unregulated and adulteration is a real hazard, so provenance matters. The banana version is fruitier and considerably more approachable.

composition.summary: Bananas, millet or cassava fermented and distilled locally.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Village pot stills, usually single distillation

composition.process: Banana waragi ferments the fruit itself, while the millet version malts the grain first.

name: Uganda Waragi
description: The commercial, juniper-flavoured version of waragi, triple-distilled and sold in bottles and sachets across East Africa. Essentially a Ugandan gin, and by far the safest way to meet the category.
funFact: It is one of East Africa's biggest spirit brands, and the sachet format was eventually banned in Uganda over concerns about street drinking.

serve.how: With tonic and lime like any gin, or with soda. The pineapple and coconut expressions are popular locally. It is lighter on juniper than a London Dry, so it takes a fruitier mixer well.

composition.summary: Triple-distilled spirit flavoured with juniper and botanicals.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper and citrus, lighter than a London Dry

composition.process: Triple distillation is a deliberate safety and consistency measure given the category's informal reputation.

name: Konyagi
description: Tanzania's own cane spirit, sold in a distinctive frosted bottle and sitting somewhere between gin and vodka in character. Legally it is neither, which suits a country that treats it as its own category.
funFact: Tanzanians often describe it as neither gin nor vodka but konyagi, and the marketing has embraced that ambiguity for decades.

serve.how: Over ice with soda, lime or coconut water. It is light enough to substitute for either vodka or gin, and locally it is drunk with bitter lemon more than anything else.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit distilled and lightly flavoured.
composition.process: It sits deliberately between categories, which is a marketing position as much as a technical one.

name: Gongo
description: Tanzanian village moonshine, distilled from maize, millet or whatever is available, and made across the country despite being illegal. Regional names change every few hundred kilometres.
funFact: Tanzania periodically runs crackdowns on gongo production, and just as periodically debates legalising and regulating it instead.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and with the same caution any unregulated distillate deserves. Quality depends entirely on whether the maker discarded the first runnings.

composition.summary: Grain or fruit fermented and distilled in improvised stills.
composition.process: Because nothing is standardised, strength and safety vary from one village to the next.

name: Ogogoro
description: Nigerian palm spirit, distilled from the sap of raffia and oil palms after it has fermented in the tree. Banned under colonial rule to protect imported gin, and now being bottled commercially with real ambition.
funFact: The British colonial administration banned it in 1909 partly to protect the market for imported Dutch and English gin, which made it a nationalist symbol.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, or infused with herbs and roots as it often is locally. The new craft bottlings are clean enough to drink like a rhum agricole and mix well with citrus.

composition.summary: Fermented palm sap distilled in pot stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sap of raffia or oil palm, fermented in the tree

composition.process: The sap begins fermenting the moment it is tapped, so distilling has to happen within a day or two.

name: Akpeteshie
description: Ghana's national spirit, distilled from palm wine or sugarcane, and outlawed by the British until independence. The name is said to mean they are hiding, from the years when making it was a criminal act.
funFact: Akpeteshie is poured on the ground as a libation to ancestors at Ghanaian ceremonies before anyone drinks any of it.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, often with a libation poured first. It is also the base for bitters infused with roots and herbs, which is how a great deal of it is consumed.

composition.summary: Palm wine or cane juice fermented and pot-distilled.
composition.process: Legalised at independence in 1957, it went from contraband to national drink almost overnight.

name: Odontol
description: Cameroonian moonshine distilled from palm wine, maize or cane, made across the country under a dozen local names. Also called arki, and produced almost entirely outside any licensing system.
funFact: Cameroon has repeatedly attempted to regulate odontol production, and the trade has repeatedly proved larger than the enforcement.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures. Frequently infused with bark and roots locally. As with any unregulated distillate, the maker's care is the only quality control there is.

composition.summary: Palm wine, maize or cane fermented and distilled informally.
composition.process: Names shift by region — odontol, arki, ha — but the method stays broadly the same.

name: Lotoko
description: Congolese spirit distilled from maize or cassava, made throughout the country in improvised stills often built from oil drums and salvaged pipe. Also called pétrole, which is not a compliment.
funFact: The nickname pétrole refers to both the colour and the smell of the roughest batches, and the comparison is not entirely unfair.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and with real caution about the source. Better-made lotoko is clean and grain-forward; badly made lotoko is genuinely hazardous.

composition.summary: Maize or cassava fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Drum and pipe stills, single distillation

composition.process: Cassava must be processed carefully first, since the raw root carries natural cyanogenic compounds.

name: Caporroto
description: Angolan artisanal cane spirit, distilled in the interior from sugarcane grown on smallholdings. A Portuguese colonial legacy crossed with local practice, and rarely bottled for export.
funFact: Angola's cane industry dates to Portuguese colonisation, and caporroto emerged alongside it as the smallholder's product rather than the plantation's.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, or with lime and sugar in the Brazilian manner, which the shared Portuguese heritage makes an obvious move. Often infused with fruit locally.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented and pot-distilled.
composition.process: Using fresh juice rather than molasses puts it technically in the agricole family.

name: Nipa
description: Mozambican distillate made from cashew fruit or palm sap, depending on the region and the season. Cashew nipa uses the fleshy apple that most of the world discards to get at the nut.
funFact: The cashew apple is highly perishable and rarely leaves the country it grows in, so distilling it is one of the few ways to use the crop at scale.

serve.how: Neat in small measures. The cashew version has a distinctive astringency that comes from the fruit itself, and locals often cut it with soft drink or fruit juice.

composition.summary: Cashew apple or palm sap fermented and distilled.
composition.process: Cashew apples must be pressed and fermented within a day of picking, which ties production to the harvest.

name: Grogue
description: Cape Verde's cane spirit, distilled from fresh juice pressed in trapiches — animal or engine-driven mills — mostly on the steep terraces of Santo Antão. Grassy, mineral and unmistakably island-made.
funFact: Santo Antão's cane is grown on terraces cut into near-vertical valleys, and much of it is still carried out by hand or donkey.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or as a grogue sour with lime and sugarcane honey. Cape Verdeans drink it at any hour and treat refusing it as slightly eccentric.

composition.summary: Fresh-pressed cane juice fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh sugarcane juice from island terraces

composition.process: Wild fermentation in open wooden vats gives grogue its funk, much as it does clairin in Haiti.

name: Ponche
description: Grogue cut with sugarcane honey and lime, sometimes with cinnamon or passion fruit added. Cape Verde's sweet counterpart to its own fierce cane spirit, and the version most visitors take home.
funFact: Mel de cana, the cane honey used to sweeten it, is boiled-down juice rather than anything made by bees.

serve.how: Neat, at room temperature or lightly chilled, after a meal. It is thick and sweet, and the passion fruit and coconut versions found on the islands are sweeter still.

composition.summary: Grogue blended with cane honey, lime and spice.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Mel de cana, lime, cinnamon, sometimes passion fruit

composition.process: Boiled cane juice gives a darker, more molasses-like sweetness than refined sugar would.

name: Malagasy Rhum
description: Madagascar distils rum from cane grown on an island that separated from Africa long enough ago to evolve its own everything. The vanilla-infused expressions draw on the world's best supply of the pod.
funFact: Madagascar produces the majority of the world's vanilla, so infusing it into local rum is less a gimmick than an obvious use of what is to hand.

serve.how: Neat or over a cube. The vanilla-infused bottlings are best served cool and neat, where the pod comes through cleanly. Younger cane spirit works well with lime and sugar.

composition.summary: Malagasy cane juice or molasses fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane grown on Madagascar, juice or molasses

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Some aged; many infused with vanilla or spice

composition.process: Whole vanilla pods are often left in the bottle, continuing to infuse after it reaches the shelf.

name: Toaka Gasy
description: Malagasy village moonshine, distilled from cane juice or rice in the highlands, technically illegal and universally drunk. The name simply means Malagasy alcohol, which tells you how central it is.
funFact: Toaka gasy production has been prohibited at various points since colonial times, largely to protect tax revenue from licensed distilleries.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, usually poured from an unlabelled bottle. It is a social and ceremonial drink in rural Madagascar, and appears at famadihana, the turning of the bones.

composition.summary: Cane juice or rice fermented and distilled in improvised stills.
composition.process: Wood-firing the still is what gives the smoke that distinguishes it from commercial rum.

name: Rhum Arrangé
description: Rum steeped with fruit, vanilla and spice, a household craft across Madagascar, Réunion and Mauritius. Every family and bar keeps its own jars, and the good ones improve for years.
funFact: On Réunion the jars sit on bar counters in plain view, and asking what is in one is a reliable way to start a long conversation.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass after a meal. It is sweeter and lower in strength than the rum it started as. Litchi, vanilla, ginger and combava are the classic infusions; the jar keeps developing as it stands.

composition.summary: Local rum macerated with fruit, spice and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Island rum, white or lightly aged

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Vanilla, litchi, ginger, combava, cinnamon, pineapple

composition.process: Time is the whole method; a jar left for a year tastes nothing like one left for a month.

name: Takamaka
description: Seychelles rum, named after the tree that lines the islands' beaches and holds the sand together. Made on Mahé from imported and local cane, and the archipelago's only spirit of any scale.
funFact: The takamaka tree is a coastal fixture across the Indian Ocean and was traditionally used for boat-building before it lent its name to a distillery.

serve.how: Over ice with coconut water or soda and lime. The aged expressions take a single cube neat. The coconut version is sweet and works better in a long drink than on its own.

composition.summary: Cane molasses and juice fermented and distilled on Mahé.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses, with some local cane juice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak for the aged range

composition.process: Tropical ageing on a small island means high evaporation and fast maturation.

name: Kachasu
description: Zimbabwean and Zambian maize moonshine, distilled in townships and rural areas from fermented maize meal. Illegal, ubiquitous, and known by a dozen names across southern Africa.
funFact: Also called junta, kachipembe or skokiaan depending on the country, and the last of those became an international hit song in the 1950s.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and with real attention to who made it. Adulteration is common, and unregulated distillation of this kind carries genuine risk.

composition.summary: Maize meal fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Maize meal, sometimes with sorghum or sugar

composition.process: The mash is soured before distillation, which is where the characteristic tang comes from.

name: Ombike
description: Namibian distillate made by Owambo communities from marula fruit, palm fruit or wild berries, using stills of clay and salvaged metal. A genuinely traditional spirit that has survived colonisation and prohibition alike.
funFact: The German colonial administration banned ombike production, and the practice continued unbroken regardless, largely because it was made by women at household scale.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, usually at social gatherings in northern Namibia. Marula ombike carries a distinct fruit note; the palm-fruit versions are earthier and rougher.

composition.summary: Wild fruit fermented and distilled in traditional stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Marula fruit, makalani palm fruit or wild berries

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Clay or improvised metal stills over open fire

composition.process: Marula fruits for only a few weeks a year, so the season dictates when the stills run.
